summary: Aircraft radios for distance, direction, landing, controllers and emergencies: what each does, its frequencies and its antenna.

blocks.title: DME: distance by timing
items: DME (Distance Measuring Equipment) times a question and its answer. The aircraft sends pulses, the interrogation; the ground station replies. A radio signal takes a measurable time to travel, so the round trip gives distance.
VORTAC: VOR plus military TACAN (tactical air navigation). Civil DME uses the TACAN's distance part.
Most DME auto-tunes to the paired VOR/LOC channel.

blocks.title: VOR: direction by phase
items: VOR (VHF Omnidirectional Range) sends 2 signals at 30 Hz: reference (FM, the same every way) and variable (AM, a pattern turning at 1800 rpm, so 30 revolutions per second).
They're in phase at 360 degrees North, magnetic. All VOR directions relate to magnetic north.
Phase difference between 2 AC voltages gives azimuth, not distance: 90° means the 090 radial.
Radials: lines drawn from the station in a magnetic direction.

blocks.title: ILS: Instrument Landing System
items: Localizer (LOC), a required part: horizontal deviation from runway center, from 2 AM patterns.
Glideslope: above or below the glide path. Selecting the localizer tunes it too.
Marker beacons beam straight up, 95% tone-modulated. The tone tells them apart.

blocks.title: ADF: finding a beacon
items: ADF (Automatic Direction Finding): loop and sense antennas swing a needle toward an NDB (Non Directional Beacon).
Signals follow the Earth's curve, over the horizon, sometimes several hundred miles.
Night effect: NDB signals bounce off the ionosphere, arriving from almost any direction.

blocks.title: Transponders
items: Mode C reports identity and altitude to ATCRBS (Air Traffic Control Radar Beacon System), encoded with pulse position modulation (PPM).
Mode S (selective) duplicates mode C and adds mid-air collision avoidance, used by TCAS.
A ground phased array radiates a 1030 MHz directional pattern.

blocks.title: On board
items: 400 Hz power: transformers, chokes and filters are smaller and lighter than in 60 Hz supplies.
Microphones: predominantly dynamic.
RF output: HF 100 W, VHF 20 W.
Ground testing radar: first clear personnel from in front of the antenna.

items.def: Traffic alert and Collision Avoidance System.
Emergency Locator Transmitter; switches on after a crash.
selective calling. A ground transmitter calls a selected aircraft or group; the crew needn't monitor the frequency.
height above the ground, from an echo.

blocks.title: Exam traps
items: Check the unit. Same digits in kHz and MHz are 1000 times apart.
Slant range isn't a bearing, glideslope angle or course width.
1800 is per minute; the answer is 30 per second.
400, 1300 and 3000 are tones in Hz, not carriers.
Patterns above and below the glide path: glideslope, not localizer.
95% AM is markers, not mode C.
